text: Yvette Chauviré (22 April 1917 – 19 October 2016) was a French prima ballerina assoluta and actress, often regarded as France's greatest ballerina, and served as the mentor to prima ballerinas Sylvie Guillem and Marie-Claude Pietragalla. She was awarded the Légion d'Honneur in 1964. Born in Paris on 22 April 1917, she enrolled in the Paris Opera Ballet school at age 10 in 1927 and was noticed for her performance in the children's ballet L'Eventail de Jeanne in 1929. At age 13, she received an invitation to join the Paris Opera ballet company. She rose through the ranks, becoming a principal dancer in 1937 and étoile in 1941. She was the star of experimental works by Serge Lifar, including Alexandre le Grand, Istar, Suite en Blanc, and Les Mirages, and studied with Russian choreographers Boris Kniaseff and Victor Gsovsky, whose influence led her toward a more lyrical style. Although not a pupil of Carlotta Zambelli, she spent considerable time observing her and adapted her techniques into her own. Lifar was accused of supporting Germany during World War II and was forced to leave the Paris Opera Ballet in 1945; Chauviré followed him to the Nouveau Ballet de Monte-Carlo. In 1947, both returned to the Paris Opera Ballet, but Chauviré left again in 1949 due to contractual disagreements over her freedom to perform with other companies. She performed in productions such as Grand pas classique (with Gsovsky for the Ballets des Champs-Elysées) and La Dame aux camélias (for the Berlin Ballet). In 1953, the Paris Opera Ballet agreed to a more flexible contract, and she returned, continuing to perform as a guest with companies in Europe, the United States, South Africa, and Latin America, often dancing with Rudolf Nureyev, who called her a "legend," and also with Māris Liepa and Erik Bruhn. During this period, she expanded her repertoire to include classical works such as Giselle, Sleeping Beauty, and The Nutcracker, with Giselle becoming her signature piece. She retired from the Paris Opera Ballet in 1956 but continued to perform with the company until 1972. From 1963 to 1968, she was co-director of the Paris Opera Ballet school and taught Guillem and Pietragalla. She also choreographed short ballets. In 1970, she became Director of the International Academy of Dance in Paris. In a 1989 interview, she criticized contemporary ballet for becoming "more and more slipshod" and warned against "extreme" movements that risk injury, stating she had always aimed to simplify within great technical difficulty. In 1992, she served as an inaugural juror for the Prix Benois de la Danse competition. She published two autobiographies: Je suis ballerine in 1960 and Yvette Chauviré – Autobiographie with Gerard Mannoni in 1997. In 1937, she performed in Jean Benoît-Lévy's film La Mort du Cygne ("The Death of the Swan"), which won the Grand Prix du Film Francais at the 1937 Paris Exposition and was released in the United States the following year as Ballerina; the film made her a star in the U.S., and she was featured on the cover of Life magazine in December 1938. In 1988, the film was rediscovered and screened in New York with Chauviré as a commentator. A documentary film, Yvette Chauviré: une étoile pour l'example, produced by Dominique Delouche, was screened at the Cannes Film Festival in 1983 and includes coaching sessions with younger ballerinas like Dominique Khalfouni and archival footage of her performances. She was married to Russian artist Constantin Nepokoitchitsky (known as Constantin Nepo), who died in 1976, and died at her home in Paris on 19 October 2016, aged 99.
